The Best Nontoxic Sunscreens, According to Dermatologists

📅 May 01, 2025  |  Category: Business  |  Read Source →

Are the best nontoxic sunscreens just marketing speak? In 2026, SPF formulas labeled as “clean” or “nontoxic” are in demand—and according to dermatologists, branding in this category isn’t mere greenwashing. “While the term ‘nontoxic’ is not strictly regulated, it’s often used to describe sunscreens that avoid certain chemical filters like oxybenzone, homosalate, and octinoxate,” says Marisa Garshick, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Manhattan and New Jersey. “Some consumers prefer this, due to concerns about irritation, allergies, or environmental impact.”

As top brands meet demand and roll out clean formulas with modern technology, nontoxic sunscreens are taking on an increasingly elegant feel, in the vein of Korean sunscreen formulas—so you can rest assured, heavy, white-cast-ridden mineral SPFs are mostly a thing of the past. Another way in which brands find a point of differentiation in the oversaturated market, as Dr. Garshick points out, is by diversifying with skincare-grade ingredients that boast benefits beyond sun protection alone. She also notes that antioxidants and hydrating ingredients, such as hyaluronic acid and glycerin, are becoming the norm in nontoxic sunscreens.

Which formulas are getting the sun-protection job done—and then some? Ahead, find the nontoxic sunscreens that dermatologists most recommend.

“There is no formal definition that qualifies something as nontoxic, but when it comes to sunscreens, it generally refers to those that don’t contain ingredients like oxybenzone or other chemical filters,” Dr. Garshick explains.

Aparovich, whose role as a biochemist at OnSkin involves safety analysis of cosmetic formulas, dives in deeper. “Nontoxic refers to a sunscreen containing no components that can be potentially detrimental to human health from the overall formulation perspective. It means that neither UV filters nor any auxiliary ingredients—such as stabilizers, emulsifiers, film-forming agents, preservatives, or fragrances—can induce known or suspected hazards, including skin irritation and sensitization, allergic reactions, endocrine disruptions, genotoxicity, and more,” she explains.

While it’s commonly thought that, in sunscreens, nontoxic refers to mineral sunscreens only, Aparovich dispels the myth. “From a human-safety standpoint, sunscreen formulas may include both mineral (physical) and/or organic (chemical) filters, with no adverse effects associated with them,” she stipulates.

Are nontoxic sunscreens as good as traditional sunscreens?

“Mineral or nontoxic sunscreens are just as effective as traditional sunscreens when used correctly,” says Dr. Day. “For my patients with eczema or psoriasis, I actually prefer them. They’re less likely to cause stinging, burning, or flares and provide excellent broad-spectrum protection.” Just like any sunscreen, she says, nontoxic ones need to be applied generously and reapplied often, especially after sweating or swimming.

Overall, Aparovich advocates looking for a sunscreen formula suited to an individual’s skin type. “People with oily, combination, or acne-prone skin should opt for products free from comedogenic ingredients to avoid clogging pores and triggering inflammation, blackheads, or breakouts,” she says. These ingredients include cacao, palm, coconut, and wheat-germ oils and chemicals like acetylated lanolin alcohol, isopropyl myristate, isopropyl linoleate, isopropyl isostearate, isopropyl palmitate, myristyl lactate, myristyl myristate, laureth-4, oleyl alcohol, and ethylhexyl palmitate.

“These are the ingredients with the highest comedogenicity rate,” she says. People with dry or sensitive skin should avoid harsh alcohols, such as alcohol, alcohol denat, ethanol, or SD alcohol, Aparovich adds. “These ingredients can compromise the skin’s barrier and cause irritation.” Additionally, she notes that an ideal nontoxic sunscreen should provide broad-spectrum protection to shield the skin from UVA and UVB rays and help reduce the risk of complex DNA damage in skin cells.

“Another key point is sunscreen’s sun protection factor, or SPF,” she says. “It indicates how effectively sunscreen can protect your skin from UVB rays, the ultraviolet light associated with sunburn.” Aparovich recommends choosing sunscreens with at least SPF 30 but ideally SPF 50, especially when the UV index is three or higher.

“Technically, there are sunscreens that claim to be 100% natural, but that term isn’t regulated,” Dr. Day says. “What matters more is that the product is clinically tested, well tolerated by sensitive skin, and free of known irritants.”

What ingredients should you avoid in sunscreen?

“Three of the most hazardous chemical filters to avoid are oxybenzone (benzophenone-3), homosalate, and octinoxate,” says Aparovich. “Studies have shown oxybenzone to be a common allergen, as well as an irritant to the eyes and skin, and a potential endocrine disruptor.” She adds that homosalate and octinoxate are linked to possible adverse effects on the endocrine system and that all three ingredients have been shown to have a negative impact on marine life and coral reefs. Additionally, Aparovich recommends avoiding formaldehyde-releasing preservatives like imidazolidinyl urea, Quaternium-15, and diazolidinyl urea, along with fragrances classified as allergenic, such as cinnamal, citral, farnesol, coumarin, eugenol, geraniol, and others. “These chemicals can trigger allergic reactions and skin irritation,” she notes. Dr. Garshick recommends seeking paraben-free products, as the ingredient can irritate some skin types.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to nontoxic sunscreens, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, SPF type, texture, packaging, finish, and the skin-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you.

Revisiting the night Marcelo Bielsa’s Bilbao blew away Fergie’s Man Utd

📅 May 01, 2025  |  Category: Sports  |  Read Source →

It was a long time coming, but late into his career English football finally became acquainted with the unique genius of Marcelo Bielsa.

His ideas, borrowed and adapted, have become part of the game here, but the man himself did not arrive on these shores until 2018 to make Leeds United a force again and end their 16-year exile outside of the top flight.

Bielsa’s Leeds made a statement in their first match back in the Premier League, losing 4-3 away to Liverpool on the opening match of the 2020-21 season. That’s not the first time a Bielsa side has given the champions of England a shock to the system.

Back in 2012, his Athletic Bilbao side unforgettably knocked Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United out of the Europa League, beating them home and away, 5-3 on aggregate.

It would be stretching it to say that Bielsa was an unknown in 2012.

Any footballing anorak with a well-worn copy of Jonathan Wilson’s Inverting The Pyramid would tell you about the Argentine establishing himself as the high priest of the high press with his revelatory Newell’s Old Boys side of the early 90s.

He was haunched on the touchline as a young Mauricio Pochettino ‘tripped’ Michael Owen to concede a penalty at the 2002 World Cup as his much-fancied Argentina side lost 1-0 to England.

And his Chile side, playing a 3-3-1-3, caught the eye at the 2010 World Cup. They suffered a group-stage exit but gave eventual champions Spain a real test.

But Bilbao was Bielsa’s first real stint in European football, save for a short-lived spell at Espanyol cut short after he was offered the Argentina job. It was long before noted Bielsistas Pochettino and Pep Guardiola would arrive in the Premier League, alongside Jurgen Klopp, to make aggressive pressing commonplace in English football.

READ: 11 of the best quotes about Marcelo Bielsa: ‘The best coach in the world’

It was an era in which Alex McLeish, Steve Kean, Alan Pardew, Martin O’Neill, Paul Lambert, Sam Allardyce, Tony Pulis, Harry Redknapp and Mark Hughes managed in the Premier League – and many of them did pretty damn well.

People actually tipped Owen Coyle to succeed Arsene Wenger at Arsenal, and David Moyes did succeed Ferguson at Manchester United.

It was long before your average football fan would have any clue what xG stood for. The sophisticated positional interplay and rabid energy of Bielsa’s best teams was just as alien.

🗣️ "I think we are in front of the best coach there is currently on the planet."

A throwback to when Pep Guardiola showered Marcelo Bielsa in praise before Barcelona faced Athletic Bilbao.

(🎥 @JimenaJuani) pic.twitter.com/gpFeMG4G8w

— Coaches' Voice (@CoachesVoice) October 29, 2019

Bielsa’s Athletic had only qualified for the Europa League after Fenerbahce had been thrown out of the Champions League for match-fixing, with Trabzonspor taking their place, thus avoiding a daunting early-season trip to Turkey for the second leg of their play-off after a goalless draw in Bilbao.

The new coach had taken time to get his ideas across in the Basque country. Athletic had taken two points from the first 15 available in La Liga and had won just five of 17 by Christmas, but they steadily improved and were fifth in the table by the time of their Round of 16 clash with Manchester United came around.

Manchester United, by contrast, had reached three of the last four Champions League finals under Ferguson and were neck-and-neck with Manchester City in the title race, eventually denied a fifth Premier League title in six years after Sergio Aguero’s iconic winner against QPR.

After dropping into the Europa League, they knocked out Eredivisie champions Ajax in the Round of 32, coming out on top against a side featuring Jan Verthonghen, Toby Alderweireld and Christian Eriksen, and were favourites for the trophy, let alone against Athletic.

That element of surprise is part of what made it so special. A sudden introduction to pure, unfiltered, glorious Bielsismo.

Around 8000 Athletic supporters made the trip to Manchester, with 6500 packed into the stands, more for the occasion and rare chance to visit Old Trafford as opposed to any real anticipation of getting a result.

The visitors had little experience, and few star names, although some (notably Javi Martinez, Ander Herrera and Fernando Llorente) were beginning to make a name for themselves.

Only goalkeeper Gorka Iraizoz and right-back Andoni Iraola were older than 26, but as a young and hungry side they had the energy and drive to execute Bielsa’s high-tempo gameplan. And so they did. This was a wild, dynamic display from the first whistle to the last.

What will no doubt be a familiar feeling to anyone that’s watched Bielsa’s Leeds over the past two years in the Championship, Athletic created chance after chance after chance but struggled to provide the final touch.

Buzzing around Ferguson’s men with the kind of constant, relentless movement that could only have been learned from Bielsa’s infamously gruelling Murderball training exercise, Athletic completely dominated at Old Trafford, pressing high and carving openings – often sending up to six men stampeding into United’s box.

“At times Barcelona can make you look silly because they keep the ball so well,” said Ryan Giggs after United were beaten 2-0 in the 2009 Champions League final. “At times we maybe chased it and didn’t keep our shape as we should have.”

It was a similar story against Athletic, who went to Manchester and recorded 61% possession by half-time (57.8% over 90 minutes), outworking and outpassing the hosts.

They did that while responding to the early setback of a 22nd-minute Wayne Rooney goal, scored against the run of play, after spurned chances from an Athletic side that came racing out of the blocks.

Were it not for profligate finishing and an excellent performance from David de Gea, Bielsa’s men might have scored three or four by the time they finally did get back on level terms, through Llorente on the stroke of half-time.

The striker worked diligently to provide a focal point and was rewarded for holding up the ball, laying it off before making his way into the six-yard box – by which point Markel Susaeta had received it on the overlap and sent it in at the perfect height for Llorente to head in.

The hosts might not have been at full-strength, with Rio Ferdinand, Paul Scholes, Michael Carrick and Danny Welbeck rested, but it was still a strong side featuring De Gea, Rafael, Patrice Evra, Chris Smalling, a Phil Jones that was still highly-rated back then, Giggs, Park Ji-Sung, with Rooney alongside Javier Hernandez in attack.

Ferguson will no doubt have subjected his players to the infamous hairdryer at the break, having seen them distinctly second best.

But it made no difference as Athletic remained on top in the second half, while introducing Carrick and Anderson early on failed to give them the foothold they so desperately lacked, looking suffocated by the visitors’ almost militaristic man-marking job.

Their pressure told for a second time, giving them a well-deserved lead in the 71st minute, Susaeta playing in Oscar De Marcos with a deftly-chipped through ball.

With two away goals and a lead to protect, they didn’t drop back, and instead just kept attacking as they did in the first minute.

That endeavour was remunerated as Iker Muniain pounced after De Gea parried out a shot from De Marcos – their 10th on target  – sprinting ahead of Rafael to slot home in injury time, sending the sizeable travelling contingent into delirium.

United’s Brazilian full-back was in position to clear the ball but stood dawdling, understandably punch-drunk after being pressed by Bielsa’s pack of wild dogs for 90 minutes.

There’d be more late drama as Rooney stepped up to score a 92nd-minute penalty, making it 3-2 on the night, giving them an unwarranted foothold in the tie, punishing an inexplicable handball from De Marcos.

But the second leg at the Sam Mames was much the same story. Total commitment and energetic pressing from Athletic. Eighteen shots to United’s two, a 2-1 win, another late consolation from Rooney.

﻿

“It was an outstanding performance by them, not only in their ability, but their energy was unbelievable,” Ferguson commented post-match.

“The highest stats of any team that has played at Old Trafford in the last 10 years, in terms of the distance run. That is great credit to the desire of the team.”

“I remember speaking to our analyst after that game. He said he had to look at the stats three times to believe them. They were off the scale,” Gary Neville later recalled.

“He’d never seen anything like it at Old Trafford.”

But the United coaches weren’t the only ones left stunned by Athletic’s performances, earning Bielsa cult hero status among Athletic’s vociferous support – like with Newell’s, fans have been known to make the pilgrimage to see his project at Leeds – and fawning praise from the British press.

“Bilbao put on a performance that has seldom been equalled by an away team at Old Trafford, blowing the hosts apart,” wrote The Guardian’s Paul Doyle.

“The champions of England were embarrassed by the superior work-rate, passing, movement and finishing of the fifth-placed team in Spain,” quipped Henry Winter in The Telegraph.

“The Argentine has breathed new life into the Basque club and its fervent support can continue to dream that their 28-year trophy drought may be about to end,” suggested Jonathan Jurejko on the BBC’s match report.

It wasn’t to be in the end, as Athletic failed to replicate their best as they lost cup finals to Barcelona and Atletico Madrid that year, but few will forget one of the best performances in the club’s history.

How To Start And Complete Arena Quests In Monster Hunter Wilds

📅 Apr 05, 2025  |  Category: World  |  Read Source →

Here's how to access arena quests, what they are, and what you'll get as rewards for doing them in MH Wilds.

The Monster Hunter series revolves around stalking your prey through lush environments, chasing them from area to area while scavenging for natural resources. However, sometimes you want your quarry to stand their ground, and Capcom developers are more than willing to cater to this play style with arena quests.

Introduced in Monster Hunter Wilds in Title Update 1, these missions shed the title's open-world focus in favor of contained bouts with the titular beasts. While these quests may seem like a walk in the park at first (after all, the monsters can't run away), you'll need to adapt to new equipment and skills if you wish to make it out alive.

Arena quests can be found in the new Grand Hub area, also introduced in Title Update 1. After speaking with Tetsuzan, you'll be able to enter the Hub by using the Peaks Back Gate in Suja.

You can also fast travel directly to the Grand Hub through the map screen.

After arriving, make your way to Ricardo at the Arena Quest Counter, positioned in the middle of the Hub. He can be found right next to Lotta, who you can use to start regular missions. Speak with him, and you'll be able to post an arena battle for you and your party.

Here's every monster in Monster Hunter Wilds!

Arena quests seem like they would be incredibly easy, considering both you and the monster are confined to an enclosed space. You won't spend any time chasing after them, and they won't be able to escape your offensive onslaught.

You can also activate the fence in the middle of the battlefield, butting the area in half and further limiting mobility.

However, you won't be operating with your normal gear. Arena quests force you to adopt preset armor and weapon combinations before starting the fight. That said, this is also a great opportunity to get some practice in with stuff outside your traditional wheelhouse.

Your pouch will also be completely different, meaning you'll only have access to the items the game gives you.

Each quest will give you a handful of equipment options; peruse the weapons and skills to find the best option for you.

Hunters are given specific equipment and item loadouts.

Hunters are allowed to use their own equipment and items.

Hunters are given specific equipment and item loadouts.

After slaying your chosen monster, you'll be rewarded with their corresponding coins. These can be spent at the forge with Gemma, where she can make brand-new armor sets. You may also earn pendants, which can be used for cosmetic customization.

Your quest rewards are based on how quickly you kill your target, so don't hold back.

Event Quests are limited in Monster Hunter Wilds, so make sure to take them on as soon as you can.

The Absolute Best Pie Recipes, According to Eater Staff

📅 Mar 12, 2025  |  Category: World  |  Read Source →

The dessert course is about to go off with a perfect pumpkin pie, chocolate peanut butter pie, a caramelized onion tart, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

We love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a big hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

“We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the New York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the New York Times

I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who says that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

How To Use A Sword And Shield In Monster Hunter Wilds

📅 Mar 02, 2025  |  Category: Other  |  Read Source →

The Sword and Shield make for a basic weapon set that is easy to learn and very rewarding to master in Monster Hunter Wilds.

With 14 different weapons to try, all of which are complex and viable, Monster Hunter Wilds offers a huge variety of gameplay styles to experience. You might be drawn to a ranged option to help keep your distance from the beasties, or maybe something complex and impressive-looking, like the Switch Axe.

If you're here, though, you might see the appeal of the humble Sword and Shield, which is an effective, user-friendly, monster-unfriendly weapon that is perfect for beginners but isn't as one-note as you might initially think. There's a lot more to this weapon than you might initially think.

Versatility is the watchword when it comes to the Sword and Shield. A skilled user of this weapon set will be able to dart around monsters easily, know when they don't need to dart around them, and deliver flurries of attacks with nimble grace.

You can see the specific Sword and Shield controls for your platform by going into Settings > Info > Play Guide > Weapon Controls > Sword and Shield.

The basic attacks of this weapon are speedy, if rather short-range. The attacks come out very quickly and are also very reactive to any movement inputs — you will be very mobile while attacking, and can even attack against some monster attacks if your timing is keen.

While this is a massive boon, it's also important to be aware of your movement inputs during a combo, as it's very easy to accidentally end up out of range thanks to some hesitancy or subconsciously moving your hunter away from the big dangerous monster in front of you.

A key aspect of the Sword and Shield is its ability to inflict both severing and blunt damage. Attacking using the Circle/B button while moving will have your hunter swinging with their shield, rather than their sword. These shield smacks deliver blunt damage that, if they hit the enemy monster's head enough, will eventually cause a knockdown.

Learning to weave shield bashes into your combos whenever you have access (and the safety!) to reach your foe's head is a great way to improve your monster hunting efficiency.

The second big selling point for this weapon is the fact that you don't have to sheath your weapon to use items, such as Potions or Antidotes. Even your Whetstone can be used with the weapon drawn.

To do this, you'll first need to hold R2/RT to raise your shield, and then press the item-use button. Using the item-use button in any other situation will just lead to you sheathing your weapon like normal.

Holding down R2/RT while using this weapon will have your hunter raise their shield in a defensive position. You can attack from this position with some low mobility but safer positions, but the main use of this technique is to reduce the damage from an incoming attack.

It's important to note that the shield this weapon provides is not the big hefty shield that other weapons might have — don't expect this shield to be able to defend against a monster's strongest attacks. Use it when you're up against light attacks, such as a Rompopolo's light jabs.

The Charge Blade is one of the more complex weapons in Monster Hunter Wilds. Here's how to master it.

While simple and easy to learn, there are some great ways to really level up your Sword and Shield gameplay, beyond just using the best Sword and Shield weapons in the game. This weapon is capable of some neat tricks.

The Sword and Shield has access to two attacks that require some charging to be used to their fullest efficacy.

The Charged Chop is a really great way to deal a ton of damage to a focused area, which is great for inflicting wounds or cutting tails. It's quite quick for a charged attack, too, so you don't necessarily need a huge opening in a monster's attack patterns to execute it.

Sliding Swipe (which is performed by hitting Triangle/Y while blocking and pressing the directional button) can also have the hunter launched into the air if they slide into a wall or ledge. Use this to your advantage with positioning and getting some aerial attacks into a fight!

But also be wary of this aspect of the ability, as getting launched into the air when you're not expecting it can be disorienting. We recommend practicing this move in the Training Camp before taking it out for a real hunt.

Not all weapons are suited to elemental affinities or status ailments, but the Sword and Shield is particularly great. This is due to the weapon being very good at delivering a very high number of attacks in a short period of time. This is especially true for status ailments.

If you're a dedicated Sword and Shield user, to the neglect of any other weapon types, a good strategy is to have two different Sword and Shields as your primary and secondary weapons. You could either stock two elements, two status ailments, or either a status or element and a strong non-elemental option. You'll have really great flexibility with this without having to sustain your skills in more than one weapon type!

This weapon's Focus Strike (which is used to destroy monster wounds and deal a lot of damage) is, shockingly enough, flexible. The initial strike into a wound (performed by aiming with L2/LT and then pressing R1/RB) will anchor your hunter onto the monster.

You can then follow the Focus Strike with either a slashing attack with Triangle/Y that deals tons of damage, or a blunt attack with Circle/B that also launches the hunter into the air and allows for a follow-up attack.

Learning when to use each variation of these attacks is a good way to really level up your gameplay with this weapon, but we've found that there's often no downside to sticking with the slashing attack variants.

There's nothing like wading in with a massive greatsword in Monster Hunter Wilds.

3 Best Walking Pad Treadmills for Homes and Offices (2026)

📅 Feb 04, 2025  |  Category: Business  |  Read Source →

Unlike bulky and almost always noisy treadmills, the best walking pads are slim (often portable) machines that can slide under your standing desk or fit anywhere in your home, letting you rack up steps while working, binge-watching, or just avoiding human interaction. Sitting at your desk all day is literally a pain. It’s terrible for your posture and takes a toll on your physical and mental health, gradually morphing you into a hunched-over keyboard gargoyle. Theoretically, you could take walking breaks away from your screen, but even then, you’re still spending a lot of the day on your butt.

I’m also convinced that walking pads make me more productive. Not only do you crush your daily steps, but regular use also boosts your energy levels, mood, and cardiovascular health. Walking on an incline also strengthens and tones your lower-body muscles, so you can even get a decent workout in. There are tons on the market, offering varying speed capabilities, extra features like built-in desk platforms and wheels, and durability. Our remote testers clocked serious hours walking, working, and sometimes jogging to find the best walking pads worth the space and money.

For more WFH gear recommendations, check out Best Standing Desks, Best Laptop Stands, and Best Office Chairs.

Updated July 2026: I’ve added a walking pad to avoid after recent safety recalls. Product information, prices, and links were also updated.

Most walking pads have similar capabilities, but the Urevo CyberPad stands out. It offers a 14-percent incline, which is one of the highest inclines on the market. WIRED contributing reviewer Kristin Canning loved that she could tackle steeper walks to get in a real workout without sacrificing her work productivity. She’s confident in the product’s durability, thanks to its solid feel underfoot and comfortable belt. It was ready to use right out of the box and painless to set up. It weighs about 71 pounds, so moving it around isn’t fun, but the wheels help.

You can control the CyberPad (and the colorful lights along the side rails) with its Bluetooth remote and app. As long as you open the app at some point during your walk, it’ll log your workout data from the machine, so you can keep track of daily step counts over time. You can also view your current workout metrics on a screen at the front of the machine.

The speed tops out at 4 mph, and the incline stops at level nine, which can be either a 9- or 14-percent incline, depending on how you position the machine’s feet. Unfortunately, the incline capability makes it difficult to store under furniture. Here’s the full review.

This is a much longer and heavier walking pad; it’s 57 inches (32.5 inches when folded), which means it’s a good choice for taller folks or anyone who has a long stride. The deck feels stable, though not as springy or as padded as the Sperax. I like the level of control and the tracking capabilities of this device more than the Sperax, though. You can adjust the speed via either the remote or the app, and you can use the pad without the app. You can check your time, speed, distance, calories, and steps on the large display.

However, this machine was a bit of a pain to set up. Getting the Bluetooth remote and KS Fit app to connect was a struggle. I also don’t like that when you first start using the machine, you have to spend time walking at slower speeds before you can “unlock” the upper end of the range. The app itself is a little wonky; if you don’t start a workout with the app, your progress won’t be tracked or logged, and it doesn’t sync later. It also saves each walking session separately, so if you take a break, you start from zero again.

The app also offers workouts, which auto-adjust the speed to your pace via sensors under the belt. It felt awkward, since I couldn’t figure out how to slow the pace without the device totally stopping. You switch between modes within the app or on the display, and you can stop and start the machine using the app or remote. I like to use the machine in manual mode, and I tend to use the app more than the remote, because the remote connectivity is inconsistent.

The machine feels like it will have a long lifespan. Its heft makes it harder to move around than the Sperax, and while the folding capability is a win in general, if you plan to slide this under something, make sure the folded height (5.4 inches) will work. Here’s my full review. —Kristin Canning

The Urevo Strol 2S Pro doubles as a treadmill and feels shockingly stable underfoot for how relatively lightweight it feels. I’ve tested several affordable treadmills, and they tend to feel wobbly at higher speeds, but this one remained firmly in place even as I ran on it at top speed and incline (7.6 mph and 9 percent). That top speed isn’t fast enough if you’re looking to really sprint, but it’s definitely ample for a good workout.

If you want to use the treadmill as a walking pad, you can keep the handrail down, which limits the top speed to 4 mph (though you can still use the full incline functionality). There’s a display on the front of the machine that cycles between time, distance, calories, incline, and speed. To access faster speeds, you have to put the handrail up, which requires you to use a hex tool to tighten it into place. The handlebar has a display as well, and you can control the machine’s basic functions from there. There’s also a tablet holder you can attach.

The machine was very easy to set up, and the remote and app connected to it right away. This app was my favorite of those I tested—it was intuitive, showed the info I wanted to see in my profile (like daily step counts), and synced well with the machine. There are some wonky translations, but nothing that bothered me or made it hard to use. As long as you open the app and connect to your treadmill at some point during your walk (even if you start and control the machine outside the app), it will log your workout data. (This isn’t the case for many of the options on this list.) In the app, you can use the Quick Start function to walk freely and adjust the settings from your phone, or you can do a virtual walk with iconic scenery.

I really appreciated how quiet this treadmill was. Overall, it seems like a durable machine that offers great value, especially with the speed and incline ranges. —Kristin Canning

This walking pad had the most intuitive setup of any on this list, most likely because of its lack of a companion app, which oftentimes feels redundant. Reviewer Kristin Canning was able to set it up in minutes, and the remote connected right away. It felt stable underfoot, even at a high incline. The remote allows you to take on 30-minute, preprogrammed walking workouts, too, where the machine auto-adjusts the speed throughout (though not the incline). Otherwise, you can use it in manual mode and adjust the settings to your liking. Unfortunately, it doesn’t track step count like some of the other walking pads I’ve tested.

The Auto Incline Walking Treadmill offers a solid incline range, going up to a level nine, or a 12-percent incline. After the Urevo CyberPad, it’s one of the highest incline capabilities I’ve found in my testing. Canning was most impressed by how quiet it is. You can connect your phone to play music through the speakers too.

NordicTrack Commercial 1750 Treadmill for $2,500: With a top speed of 12 mph, incline and decline options, a springy running deck, fans, a 16-inch pivoting touchscreen, and two water bottle holders, this is the best treadmill tester Kristin Canning has used. Although it is a foldable treadmill and suitable for walking and hiking workouts, it’s still bulky and relatively expensive if you’re only looking for a space-saving walking pad. If you’re searching for a running treadmill, check out Canning’s guide to the Best Treadmills.

Toputure TP6 Walking Pad for $238: This is a foldable, screenless walking pad that is ideal for small apartments and spaces. It takes only a few minutes to set up and compact, but it weighs 56 pounds, so it’s not the most portable. During my second day of testing, the pad began making a high-pitched scraping noise, which likely indicated a misaligned belt. This unbearable noise would come and go throughout my two weeks of testing. The handlebars are height-adjustable, ranging from 32 to 45 inches, and they are also tilt-adjustable. Be aware of the handlebar locks while walking by, as they can catch on clothing. As a budget option, I still prefer the Sperax, which is a couple of dollars cheaper.

Urevo SpaceWalk 5L Smart Walking Pad for $400: We’ve tested a couple of Urevo walking pads, and while the SpaceWalk 5L is decent and cheaper, we still prefer the CyberPad for Home for its 14 percent incline and the Strol 2S Pro for its speed and ability to double as a treadmill. The SpaceWalk 5L has a larger weight capacity, maxing out at 300 pounds, with the same incline as the Strol 2S Pro (9 percent) and max speed as the CyberPad (4 mph). Its track length is a solid 39 inches, and WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani said it’s compact enough to stash underneath a couch or loveseat.

Lifesmart TM2202 3-in-1 Treadmill for $699: The 3-in-1 Treadmill gets its name from its ability to serve as a walking pad (with the rail down, the speed tops out at 3.7 mph), a treadmill (with the rail up, you can run up to 7.5 mph), and a workstation (with the rail up and desk attachment on) for multitasking. It’s easy to set up, and switching between modes is quick and simple (you just need to use a small tool to adjust the rail; the tool is magnetized, so it can live on the rail and never get lost in a junk drawer). The desk’s height won’t accommodate everyone; it was lower than I’d like, and I’m 5'4". But for quick, basic work like answering emails or sitting in on a meeting, it got the job done just fine. It also doesn’t have any incline options. —Kristin Canning

GoYouth 2-in-1 Under Desk Treadmill for $270: This is an Amazon top pick, but it’s very bare-bones for this price. There’s no app, and the remote and controls are unintuitive. The built-in Bluetooth speaker sounds unsurprisingly crappy. But it does feel great underfoot, is very quiet, and has a higher weight capacity (300 pounds) and a slightly longer belt than the Sperax above. If you’re a larger person looking for a simple, affordable walking pad, this will work for you. —Adrienne So

Egofit Walker Pro M1 for $479: This is one of the first walking pads we’ve tested, and it has a fixed 5 percent incline that might pose some storage issues (you won’t be able to just slide it under the couch). It can be controlled via an app or a remote, but it doesn’t automatically sync if you use the remote. But it’s lightweight and easy to move around your home.

Sperax Walking Pad: The US Consumer Product Safety Commission has warned consumers to stop using several Sperax walking pad and treadmill models due to the fall and fire hazards they pose. According to the CPSC, the machines can unexpectedly change speeds or come to a sudden stop, and there have also been reports of overheating and fires. The warning applies to the Pro, Q1, RM-01, and RM-02 models, but I’d avoid this brand altogether.

Size and storage: Walking pads are typically much smaller than traditional treadmills, but check the product dimensions and make sure the footprint will work for you. If you’re working with an especially small space, consider a foldable or under-desk walking pad. If you’re planning to store it under furniture or in a closet when not in use, shop for slimmer models with wheels for portability.

Belt size and track length: The size of your track is dependent on the product’s dimensions, and you should take into consideration how much space you have to work with. But, generally, I prefer wider and lengthier belts that feel more stable to walk on, especially if you’re on the taller side or have a longer stride.

Weight capacity: Walking pads aren’t as durable as treadmills and tend to have a lower weight capacity. Check the machine’s limit, and make sure it will work for you and anyone else in the household who will be using it. Per the online reviews we’ve read, walking pads are notorious for falling apart after only a few years or even a few months of use, so it might be worth getting something that’s a little more heavy-duty.

Speed range: Choose a walking pad that offers a speed range that best fits your lifestyle and goals. Most models will generally offer speeds up to 4 mph, which should cover everything from gentle strolls and brisk walks, and is ideal for home office use. There are walking pad-treadmill hybrids that offer faster paces if you’re also looking for a jog.

Adjustable inclines: Some models remain flat, but I prefer the walking pads that feature adjustable levels so that you can customize your cardio intensity as you see fit. Walking at an incline can also strengthen your lower body muscles and reduce anterior knee loading.

Metrics and display: Most walking pads have an LED display that tracks your steps, distance, time, and calories. Some models also include a remote control and/or app, which can sometimes sync your metrics from the machine, so you can check your workout data on your phone. This may not matter to you if you prefer to use your Apple Watch or fitness tracker.

Price: You can snag a solid, no-frills walking pad for under $200, but if you’re looking for a higher-end model with a surplus of features, it can cost $500+.

Our remote team members evaluated each walking pad from their own home offices, using the pads during real workdays. Testers of different heights, stride lengths, and lifestyles walked for hour-plus stretches while answering emails, taking meetings, and performing other work-related tasks; we noted how each pad felt over time and whether any annoyances surfaced with prolonged use. We evaluated every model for at least two weeks across the following criteria:

I’ll be testing the DeerRun Q2 Urban Smart Walking Pad and the GoPlus 2-in-1 Folding Treadmill. I’m also reevaluating Urevo CyberPad for Home.

The 15 Best War Miniseries of All Time, Ranked

📅 Jan 31, 2025  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

TV miniseries can cover a wide array of topics, from horror to drama, to romance, and even to war. War miniseries are definitely not super common, as war is generally more of a movie thing due to the demanding production value that the genre entails, but that's not to say that many war miniseries haven't come to exist in the age of television. From various countries, networks, and streaming platforms, these miniseries tell a whole lot of stories, ranging from Medieval conflicts to modern warfare.

Many of these series have generated a lot of buzz and have drawn a lot of critical attention due to their outstanding quality, sweeping dramatic flair, or entertainment value, delivering their messages in gradual, bite-sized formats that don't overstay their welcome nor exit too soon. These are the best war miniseries ever made, which any fans of the war movie genre should definitely check out.

Generation War, known as Our Mothers, Our Fathers in its native Germany, is a three-part miniseries set during the Second World War. The series has been the topic of a lot of hot debate, as it follows the perspective of the Nazis and has a lot of major historical inaccuracies. However, it is also undoubtedly well-made and technically impressive, though its hiccups are pretty major.

Some criticized it for its inability or unwillingness to show the Nazis' true motive of purging the world of anyone they deemed unworthy, while others praised it for its harrowing drama and fantastic action. One thing is for sure: this is not a show that is for everyone. But for the right audience, who don't mind delving into some hot-button issues and a fresh stain on the history of Germany, it's pretty enjoyable.

Women at War is a Franco-Belgian miniseries created for Netflix. It is set during World War I and focuses on the lives of four very different women on the home front rather than in active combat. One is a nurse, one is a prostitute, one is a nun, and the last is a factory worker. Though many of them have troubled pasts and some are even actively on the run from law enforcement, their destinies intertwine, and they all wind up supporting the war effort as much as they can.

Generally, World War I shows or movies tend to hone in on the combat, as that's where the most action is. However, Women at War allowed the untold stories of conflict to come to light and show how massive an undertaking the effort was, with ordinary people having to sew uniforms, work in factories, or serve as nurses in military hospitals. Not only does the show emphasize the massive scale of the war and how everybody was forced to help out, but it also shows that women did indeed have an important role in the conflict, even if they weren't on the front lines.

All the Light We Cannot See was positively annihilated by critics, earning scathing reviews and harsh criticisms. But most audiences were a lot nicer to it, earning a divisive score of 27% for critics, but 81% for audiences on Rotten Tomatoes, which might be one of the biggest differences in scores in television. To be fair, this miniseries, based on the novel by Anthony Doerr, was not without its fair share of questionable choices or rough moments.

The four-part story is set in occupied France during World War II, where a blind French woman living in the shadow of the Third Reich whose life intersects with a Wehrmacht soldier who was forcibly conscripted into the military. It may not be the most technically amazing miniseries ever, with some major changes from its source material, and its inability to capture the real emotional depth of the book, but many audiences still found it entertaining, although far from the best thing out there.

Set during the First World War, Birdsong may be short at a mere two episodes, but this miniseries was viewed by millions in its home country of the United Kingdom, and presents a very emotional story in spite of its meager runtime. The show stars Eddie Redmayne and Clémence Poésy as Stephen and Isabelle, respectively. Stephen is a British soldier overseas in France fighting in the Great War, while Isabelle is a French woman living in the countryside who becomes the subject of a love affair with Stephen.

Portraying forbidden love and nightmarish trench conditions in equal measure, Birdsong may not be as famous as some of the other miniseries, but it is emotionally moving, all the same. This one is definitely more of a drama than an action flick, though, so be prepared for something different. Fans of the show commended it for how beautifully it captured the essence of the war and of love, and for the heartfelt performances of its principal cast.

Shōgun is more commonly known for the 2024 TV show based on James Clavell's novel; however, while it began as a miniseries, it is receiving a second season, thus it no longer fits the criteria for this list. In any event, the five-part 1980 miniseries is still amazing on its own. It serves as a perfectly fine (and much more faithful) adaptation of the source material.

The miniseries is set during the dawn of the Edo Period of Japan, which was marked by civil war, political upheaval, and constant societal unrest. It is more commonly known as "Feudal Japan." Though all of the characters and events in this show are fictional, they are inspired by real historical figures. Shōgun is a great show if you like political dramas, Japanese history, or this turbulent period of time that became so internationally famous.

Catch-22 is a satirical dark comedy set during World War II and is once again based on a novel, this time by Joseph Heller. There was a 1970 film adaptation of the book, which is a very good film, so hopes weren't very high for the miniseries. Yet the show is just as good as the movie, sporting a whole new cast and updated filming techniques, making it feel a lot more polished and poignant. Story-wise, it's about a United States Air Force bombardier who is frustrated with the amount of dangerous missions he is being sent on, so tries to weasel his way out of the military through a series of legal loopholes.

There are some heavy hitters in this show, including George Clooney and Hugh Laurie, among others, with much of the action centering on the Mediterranean Theatre of the war. Catch-22 was nominated for two Golden Globes and two Emmys, yet amazingly, didn't win any of them. Regardless, a nomination is more than enough to speak to its quality, which is matched by its high critical scores and rave reviews.

The White Queen is based on Philippa Gregory's novel of the same name, which is set during the Wars of the Roses. This historical conflict took place at the end of the Middle Ages and involved a Civil War in England involving the Royal Houses of Tudor and Lancaster versus the House of York in a series of attempts to seize the throne. The result was a victory for the House of Tudor, from which the current British royal family is descended.

While the conflict itself is pretty famous worldwide, often focusing on Medieval warfare and sword-and-shield combat, what is less famous is the role of women behind the scenes, which is what this story is about. The White Queen examines how many of the royal women pulled strings and executed a series of daring political maneuvers to ensure victory for their house. It might not be the most action-packed series, but it's a fantastic Medieval political drama that deserved every ounce of praise it received.

A Small Light is an eight-part miniseries set during World War II, and the accompanying genocide known around the world as the Holocaust. The main character is Miep Gies (Bel Powley), a Dutch secretary who worked for Otto Frank (Liev Schreiber). Otto Frank is, of course, the father of Anne Frank (Billie Boullet), whose diary became an international sensation after her death. As many already know, the Frank family was Jewish, making them a primary target of the Third Reich's genocide. Gies, being a Christian, risked her life to hide the family from the Nazis.

Even though she was eventually discovered and the Frank family was abducted, with Anne dying in a labour camp shortly thereafter, Gies is still regarded as a hero for putting everything on the line to do what was right. It provides an interesting new perspective on one of the most famous historical accounts of the Third Reich's evil, and shows how anyone can be a hero in their own way. Of course, one should take warning, though, as this is obviously a real tear-jerker.

Masters of the Air serves as a companion piece to the classic miniseries Band of Brothers, taking audiences high above occupied Europe during World War II, where a British bombing squadron conducts a series of raids against key locations to the Allied war effort. With a new cast of younger, rising actors like Austin Butler and Barry Keoghan, Masters of the Air is a welcome return to the small screen for the Band of Brothers universe, and is proof that it hasn't lost its charm, even all these years later.

Winning the Emmy for Outstanding Sound Design, Masters of the Air offered a fresh spin and a new perspective on some of the most classic war stories, allowing audiences to see them with a bird's-eye view, experiencing the tragedy and hardships that Royal Air Force members experienced above the clouds of the tumult on the ground. There are some huge inaccuracies regarding its historical aspects, but in terms of sheer entertainment value, Masters of the Air is definitely up there.

Chief of War is something of a passion project for creator and star Jason Momoa. Owing to Momoa's Hawaiian heritage, the story is set in the 19th Century, during a time when the Hawaiian Islands had yet to become a part of the US. The islands were fragmented into four kingdoms, with one of the most famous being the kingdom of Maui, which was ruled by Kamehameha I (Kaina Makua).

The series follows Ka'iana (Momoa), a historic Hawaiian warrior who served under Kamehameha I, waging a bloody conquest against the other island kingdoms after returning home from a long journey. Chief of War is such an authentic miniseries, with versions in both English and Hawaiian, for that extra level of immersion. Better yet, it talks about a historical conflict that is often ignored or left out of history books, yet is rich and fascinating.

Who Are The Clarks & Newmans In Black Doves? Crime Families Explained

📅 Dec 11, 2024  |  Category: Business  |  Read Source →

WARNING: SPOILERS ahead for Black Doves season 1.

The Clarks and the Newmans are two feared and dangerous London-based crime family organizations in the Netflix espionage series Black Doves. Created by Joe Barton (The Lazarus Project, Giri/Haji), Black Doves has outstanding reviews, earning a 98% Rotten Tomatoes critic score after its December 5, 2024 release date. Knightley (Atonement, Pirates of the Caribbean) leads the cast of Black Doves along with Ben Whishaw's Sam Young, best known for playing Q in Daniel Craig's James Bond films. Black Doves features a stellar supporting cast, including Sarah Lancashire's Reed, Kathryn Hunter's Lenny, and Ella Lily Hyland's Williams.

Black Doves follows public figure Helen Webb, the loving and supportive wife of Andrew Buchan's Wallace Webb, a prominent British politician. Webb is also a secret agent working for the mysterious covert spy organization known as the Black Doves, which Mrs. Reed is the head of. Reed confronts Helen over an affair she was having with a civil servant named Jason (Andrew Koji), who was shockingly shot and killed in a park from long range. Suspecting that Helen could be in hot water with a powerful criminal conspiracy headed by the notorious Clark family, Reed enlists a trusted triggerman named Sam Young for assistance.

In Black Doves season 1, the Clarks and the Newmans are two separate organized crime families who operate out of London, England. The Newmans are the first of the two crime families to be introduced in the series through a flashback involving Sam several years before the main plot of the series takes place. As one of Sam's early assignments after Lenny ordered him to take out his father, Frank, for his first hit, Sam kills three of the four Newman brothers who were starting to make a name for themselves as drug dealers. The Newman brothers were a violent group of drug dealers with quite a gang at their disposal. Young Hector launched an attack on Sam with this gang to seek revenge for his brothers. He's played by Luther Ford.

The Clarks are a much bigger crime family conglomerate out of London. They have international outreach and have established connections in several countries, including the United States. Alex Clark was the head of the Clark family mob before Sam killed her at the end of Black Doves season 1. Her son, Trent Clark, was not a prominent figure in the organization apart from being Alex's son. He appears to be of little use to Alex in the series but is the main reason why several of the deaths take place, most significantly Ambassador Chen, who he accidentally killed, and Jason, who he hired another assassin named Elmore Fitch to murder.

Alex Clark, played by Tracey Ullman, is the London crime boss and the Clark matriarch in Black Doves. Her son, Trent, is meant to be her successor in the business. Helen confronts Alex in a showdown late in the season, and Alex claims she had no part to play in the death of Jason Davies.

Hector was the boy who Sam let live, which forced him to walk away from the assassin business and get out of London for seven years. When Sam returns to London, Lenny gets a hold of him and wants him to make good on the botched hit on Hector Newman, who had grown up and expanded his own profitable drug ring. Lenny still found Hector to be a nuisance in London even after all those years and forced Sam to make good on his promise. Newman had gotten more powerful and disruptive after Sam let him off the hook.

Sam didn't pull the trigger on Hector when he had the chance because he was just a kid and that would have violated his own moral code as a hitman. Apart from Hector, Black Doves season 1 doesn't introduce any other prominent Newmans, indicating that Hector may be the last man standing in his crime family. Hector's operation was weakened after the Clarks took out dozens of his men searching for Kai-Ming, Ambassador Chen's daughter. This is why Hector doesn't kill when he has the chance and why he shows up at Michale's apartment asking to join forces at the end of the season. Hector also thanks Sam for killing his bully brothers and offers him a job.

Trent Clark is the main reason why the entire plot unfolds in Black Doves and is why Ambassador Chen, Jason, Maggie, Phillip, Stephen Yarrick, and even Elmore Fitch, were all killed. Despite his pleas for innocence and his admission of guilt in the Black Doves season 1 finale, Trent had far too much blood on his hands. In the final moments of Black Doves season 1, Sam sensed that Helen was about to take revenge on Trent for killing Jason and taking more lives trying to cover it up. Sam takes out Trent, Alex, and their bodyguard so Helen doesn't bring danger to her family. In the Black Doves season 1 finale, Sam shoots Alex and then kills Trent before Helen has a chance to pull the trigger herself. He appears to be sparing her the burden of being a killer like him. A distraught Helen says Trent was hers to kill.

There's nothing really tragic about Trent's death since he is by far the most irredeemable character in the series. The same can be said for Alex Clar, who was completely unaware that Trent was trying to cover himself by ordering hits on everyone who knew about Ambassador Chen's death. While Alex and Trent are not featured much in Black Doves season 1, and won't be included in the eventual season 2, their deaths could spell trouble for Helen and Sam in future episodes.

If anything, the Clarks and the Newmans are rival crime families with very different levels of power and scale. The Clarks are internationally recognized, while the Newmans, or at least what's left of them with Hector, are a more local clan operating in the United Kingdom. Hector Newman may have additional connections throughout Europe since his primary trade appears to be selling and distributing drugs.

One of the biggest mysteries in Black Doves season 1 is how Hector Newman came to find Kai-Ming in the first place and why she was stuck in his warehouse. Since the Clarks were looking for Kai-Ming and shot up the Newmans' warehouse, it wouldn't make sense if the two crime families were operating on the same team. It's more than likely that the Newmans and the Clarks are rival gangs, although the Clarks are much more sophisticated than the Newmans in the first season. Since Alex Clark is dead, Hector Newman could try to gain power among the Clarks or enlist some of their henchmen and resources to expand his organization in Black Doves season 2.

After discovering her lover's murder, a spy masquerading as a politician's wife joins forces with an old assassin associate to uncover the truth and seek revenge.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Factually inaccurate: Alex Clark was not the head of the crime family, this is stated explicitly by her and about her.

KaiMing ended up with Hector Newman because she freaked out when she found out that her father's dead in her apartment. Then she ran to her drug dealer's place, which apparently turn out to be a warehouse/club owned by Hector.

The Vogue Business Funding Tracker

📅 Nov 13, 2024  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Introducing the Vogue Business Funding Tracker, a running list highlighting the most notable and intriguing investment and M&A activity in fashion and beauty. From emerging disruptors to legacy giants undergoing major changes, we spotlight the deals that are shifting the dynamics of the sectors we cover, including fashion, beauty, tech and sustainability.

Company description: Republic Brands Group has acquired Rebecca Minkoff, which was founded by Minkoff and her brother Uri in 2005. The acquisition comes as the brand enters a new phase of growth following a successful transition to an asset-light licensing model, according to the company. Republic Brands plans to expand the brand’s international footprint and retail partnerships, with the view of doubling the business in 2027. Minkoff, who is chief creative officer, will remain closely involved in the brand’s creative direction under its new ownership.

Investor(s): Republic Brands Group (portfolio includes: Jason Wu, Christian Siriano, Joie)

Investor comments: “Rebecca Minkoff represents exactly the type of brand we believe has tremendous untapped potential,” Sami Souid, founder and CEO of Republic Brands Group, said in a statement. “It has strong consumer recognition, an authentic design identity and significant opportunities for global expansion. Our strategy is to unlock that potential through best-in-class operating partners, disciplined brand management and a focused approach to building a global lifestyle business.”

Company description: Founded in 2023, Counsel Health is an AI-powered primary care platform that combines medical AI with a network of physicians to deliver personalized medical guidance and treatment. The company has agreed to be acquired by Finnish smart ring maker Oura for $625 million, as Oura looks to move beyond biometric tracking toward more holistic, tailored health insights and actionable medical care. The acquisition will integrate Counsel’s AI and on-demand physicians with Oura’s continuous health data collection, enabling users to access medical advice, prescriptions, lab result interpretations, and chronic care support through the Oura app.

Funding and round: Acquisition, $625 million.

Investor comments: “Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale. “Together, we can create a new model of care that extends the current healthcare paradigm by delivering an experience that’s more immediate, personalized, and proactive.”

Company description: Founded in 1889, Lee has made its marks as one of the biggest heritage names in denim. The American brand generates an average of $1.5 billion in annual sales across 73 countries, of which almost 40% comes from outside the US and Canada. New York-based Authentic Brands Group has successfully acquired Lee from Kontoor Brands in an effort to expand Lee into adjacent categories, including activewear and workwear, as well as lifestyle offerings.

Investor(s): Authentic Brands Group (portfolio includes: Guess, Juicy Couture, Reebok).

Investor comments: “We are thrilled to welcome Lee to the Authentic family,” said Jamie Salter, founder and executive chair of Authentic Brands Group. “Lee has the heritage, recognition and consumer loyalty we look for in a brand. By connecting Lee to Authentic’s global platform and the right partners in key markets, we see a significant opportunity to expand its reach through content, experiences and new product categories.”

Company description: Touted as London’s first functional smoothie bar, Elevate launched at the Royal Exchange in June 2025, before opening in Selfridges in April 2026. Founded by Julia Baldet, its bestselling smoothie, The Glow, made with collagen and hyaluronic acid, has grossed close to half a million pounds since rollout. Elevate has collaborated with brands such as Nike x Skims, Adanola, Ouai and Medicube, as wellness continues to crossover into beauty and fashion. The new funding will be used to open additional London sites next year, after finishing its first full year with over £1 million in sales.

Investor(s): JamJar (portfolio includes: Innocent Drinks, Deliveroo, Humantra), Active Partners (portfolio includes: Tala, Healf, Salad Project) Cassius, Soho House founder Nick Jones.

Investor comments: “Elevate’s proposition is perfect: delicious smoothies that look great while meeting real nutritional and wellness needs. It’s clearly working; loyal customers love the brand. But most of all, we’re backing Julia. She’s focused, ambitious, creative and commercial, and we’re thrilled to support her as she builds Elevate into a category-defining brand,” JamJar partner Adam Balon said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has successfully taken control of Hugo Boss. Following a rejected takeover bid of €2 billion (€38 per share) in June, the British retail conglomerate has raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company will now become a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned business.

Hugo Boss believed the June takeover proposal to be “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Though Frasers continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding once again to 48% in mid-August (up from 30.3% in June, alongside the initial takeover bid). Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position last month, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4% to 6%. This comes after the growing British retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% last week, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. This marks a potential pullback from its current luxury brand spending spree.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has acquired a 8.78% stake in US-based sports brand Under Armour, continuing a string of cross-category investments in recent months. Earlier this week, Frasers upped its investment in Burberry to 6.3%, having also taken on ownership of esteemed department store Harvey Nichols in August. The Frasers portfolio spans discount retailer Sports Direct through to The Webster, House of Fraser, and Flannels, as well as a strong stake in Hugo Boss — upped to 47.89% in August. Under Armour’s share price has risen since the SEC filing was made on October 1.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct, The Webster)

Company description: Frasers Group has upped its economic interest in Burberry from 4.2% to 6.3%, with the British brand now part of a new luxury division launched in early October. Also part of the luxury portfolio, Hugo Boss — of which Frasers now owns almost 48% — continues to reject the retail group’s takeover bids; it may be looking elsewhere for potential acquisitions.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct).

Company description: Activewear brand 437 was founded in 2016 by co-CEOs Adrien Bettio and Hyla Nayeri. Initially founded as a swimwear brand, 437 moved into activewear in 2023, which is now the core of its business. The Toronto-based brand is the top-selling activewear brand on Revolve, and has fast become a celebrity go-to.

Funding and round: $15 million CAD, minority stake

Investor(s): Revolve (portfolio includes: Alliance Apparel, Alexandre Vauthier)

Investor comments: “437 is still a small player, but is already outselling nearly every activewear brand on our site, including billion dollar brands. The brand is great and the aesthetic and products are great — it’s really just building on their core momentum and continuing to gain awareness. Hyla and Adrien had built something very special, but had also reached a point where they needed additional capital, infrastructure, and a thought partner who had been through the same journey,” said co-founder and co-CEO Michael Karanikolas.

Company description: Founded by former fashion executive Yasmin Sewell, Vyrao launched in 2021 as a fragrance brand blending aromatherapy and neuroscience principles. The brand was ahead of the curve tapping into the cross-section of fragrance and wellness, by offering customers something more than just a scented mist. Following the acquisition, the genderless brand will embark on its next development phase under its new owner.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Company description: Based in LA, Arey launched in 2021 under entrepreneur Allison Conrad and celebrity hairstylist Jay Small, offering vitamin, antioxidant and peptide-infused products to help delay and repigment aging hair. The funding will support Arey’s new product development, ongoing clinical research, and expansion through retail partnerships.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever Ventures (portfolio includes:), Greycroft, Female Founders Fund.

Company description: AI-driven discovery platform Slayd launched in Gurugram, India, in 2025. Targeted at Gen Z, the startup sorts fashion items from more than 300 marketplaces and brands by theme and curates personalized feeds that enable product discovery across multiple sites. Slayd claims to currently have more than 200,000 users, and can identify emerging trends through its proprietary tech software. The investment will help strengthen its team and accelerate the growth of its private-label business, Slayd Originals.

Investor(s): AJVC (portfolio includes: Midcase, Bubble Me, Trufides).

Company description: ISDIN is a product of pharmaceutical company Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve (CQFE) and beauty group Puig, who partnered to launch the skincare brand in 1975. Since then, both families have supported ISDIN’s evolution into a global dermatological skincare business focused on scientific formulation and innovation. In acquiring CQFE’s 50% stake, Puig will obtain complete ownership of the Spanish brand.

Investor(s): Puig (portfolio includes: Charlotte Tilbury, Byredo, Penhaligon’s, Dr. Baraba Sturm).

Investor comments: “Expanding our presence in dermocosmetics is a strategic priority for Puig. ISDIN is a unique company, with a strong management team, a clear strategy and a distinctive position in dermatology and skincare. Full ownership will give Puig the best platform to support its next phase of growth and continue investing behind the science and innovation that have made ISDIN successful,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa said.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Talm (“To All the Mamas”) initially focused on bodycare products during pregnancy and postpartum, however the brand has gradually expanded to offer sensitive skincare for all stages of life. It currently offers around a dozen products, operates in roughly a dozen countries, and reports double-digit revenue growth. This marks the first acquisition for Caudalie, which plans to accelerate Talm’s global expansion and product development by leveraging its pharmacy network, sales force and infrastructure.

Company description: Medici Brands, owner of David Protein and newly launched confectionery brand HallPass, will use its Series B funding to enter the next phase of growth. This includes expanding HallPass’s retail presence, alongside the remainder of its product portfolio — extending David into new formats and categories, advancing product innovation, and enabling the launch and scaling of new brands such as Rowdy.

Funding and round: $250 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Greenoaks (portfolio includes: Stripe, Canva, Discord, Robinhood), Valor Equity Partners (portfolio includes: GoPuff, SpaceX, BitGo), Peter Rahal, Iconiq, Imaginary Ventures.

Investor comments: “Two years ago, David Protein showed customers they no longer had to choose between great macros and great taste, and it became one of the fastest-growing CPG brands in America. Now, Medici is bringing that approach to the rest of the store, building a house of brands that delivers the taste consumers adore, without making the compromises they have grown to accept,” said Greenoaks partner Neil Shah.

Company description: Truly Beauty is a plant-based personal care brand founded in 2013 by Maxx Appelman. Known for its viral, Gen Z-focused bodycare and social media marketing, Truly Beauty combines high-performing active ingredients with a luxurious but playful aesthetic. It is headquartered in Los Angeles. For razor company Dollar Shave Club, this marks its first acquisition as it extends beyond grooming.

Investor comments: “By layering Truly’s fast-turn product engine onto our AI-driven inventory planning and backend logistics, we are building a high-velocity innovation model that legacy CPG conglomerates simply cannot replicate,” said Dollar Shave Club CEO Larry Bodner.

Company description: Scottish-born accessible luxury leather goods brand Strathberry has closed its second funding round, consisting of a growth investment from Soho Square Capital’s new Fund II, and marking the fund’s first investment. The funding comes on the heels of a strong year for Strathberry, which delivered 39% year-on-year growth in 2026 at $50.5 million. Soho Square’s investment will support Strathberry founders Guy and Leeanne Hundleby’s ambitions to accelerate the brand’s North America expansion.

Funding and round: Undisclosed minority investment valuing the company at approximately £100 million, second funding round.

Investor(s): Soho Square Capital’s Fund II.

Investor comments: “Strathberry is an exceptional brand with a rare combination of craftsmanship, a distinctive design signature and a genuinely international, loyal customer base. The label’s ‘high-end quality at accessible prices’ ethos is resonating with shoppers disillusioned with top luxury houses. Guy, Leeanne, and the team have created something special, and there is significant scope to grow the business internationally,” Soho Square Capital director David Steel said in a statement.

Company description: Thorne, the science-backed supplements brand founded in 1984, has entered into a definitive acquisition agreement with P&G. Thorne is currently owned by L Catterton’s Flagship Fund. It is now best known in the wellness space for its creatine product, leaning into the rise of the supplement and its various formats. The acquisition helps to further Thorne’s attempt at becoming the market’s most-trusted personalized health brand, as well as P&G’s aim to move its personal health business upmarket. The transaction is expected to close later this year, subject to regulatory approval.

Investor(s): Procter & Gamble (portfolio includes: Seven Seas, Oral-B, Pepto Bismol).

Investor comments: “Consumer interest in selfcare, prevention, wellness, and personalized health continues to grow, and Thorne strengthens our position in premium wellness with a trusted, science-backed brand that complements our existing portfolio,” CEO of P&G Health Care Paul Gama said.

Company description: Frasers Group has taken a 4.2% position in British luxury brand Burberry. Frasers, the company behind House of Fraser, Sports Direct and Flannels, is holding the position through put options, which gives Frasers Group the right to buy shares at a predetermined stock price. The company is also the second largest shareholder in Mulberry PLC.

Frasers Group has been on an investing spree of late, increasing its stake in Hugo Boss to 30.3% and offering a takeover proposal. Frasers Group also bought Matches for £52 million in December 2023, before it announced that it was going into administration; Matches was sold in December 2025 to form part of newly established luxury group Hulcan.
